messages.subject: [statnet_help] Random Number Non-Mixing Chains
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet community,

I am working on a simulation study that involves simulating and estimating
a large amount of ERGMs. I encountered some weird behavior in the
estimation that I cannot explain.
While estimating 100 networks (30 nodes, average degree 8, reciprocity
~.30, transitivity ~.3, 70% homopholous ties) with the exact model that I
used to simulate them, about 45 of the networks gave an error:
"Unconstrained MCMC sampling did not mix at all. Optimization cannot
continue."

I took one of the networks giving the error and estimated it 100 times with
100 randomly selected random number seeds. Of those 100 estimations, 21
gave the same error.

Is there a way to avoid this problem, other than catching it with
tryCatch() and letting the code re-run with a different random number seed?

Best Regards,

Robert Krause

ICS Sociology, PhD Student
University of Groningen
Grote Rozenstraat 31,
Room B119
9712 TG Groningen, The Netherlands

Dear list members,

 

I am new to R and statnet and only did ergm analyses with PNet before. Now,
I would like to reproduce my analyses in statnet. Specifically, I try to run
ergms for a directed network of 138 actors. but encounter a problem when
including the "mutual" parameter in combination with one of my quantitative
vertex attributes. The term I use is mutual(by="name of the attribute"). The
model begins to run, but produces an error shortly after indicating "R
encountered a fatal error. The session was terminated.". This problem occurs
also with other quantitative attributes. When I run the model without the
vertex attribute - for standard mutual statistic - it works fine. I do not
get any error for the nodeicov/nodeocov parameter together with the same
vertex attributes either. Does anyone know if there is something wrong with
my syntax or what else could be the problem?

 

Any help would be highly appreciated!

 

Best,

messages.body_plain:
Hey Natalie,

I understand your decision to incorporate them in one network. Comparing
parameters of network models with varying sample size and density is very
difficult, if not quite impossible.

First, could you take a look if all of these sub networks are not
degenerate or completely mutual? It could be that one of your groups has
only reciprocated ties. this could lead to computational problems.
Second, it might be an idea to add a general mutual term. Because mutual by
is an interaction of mutual and the covariate, and having interactions
without both main effects is rather odd (although I understand your
decision here, for there are no ties between groups). I have not used
mutual(by =) in ergm so I might be wrong about this...
Third, it might help if you fix your gwesp parameter and not estimate a
curved exponential random graph. E.g: gwesp(alpha = log(2),fixed = TRUE,
cutoff = 30)
Related, I found that triadic structures are better captured if next to
gwesp gwdsp is also included -> gwdsp(alpha = log(2), fixed = TRUE, cutoff
= 30)

Unfortunately these might nit fix your problem after all. To be sure, your
computer has enough free working memory?

It might be an idea to run the model without the control part. You might
not get a converging model, but if you do not encounter the error, we are
closer in finding where it comes from.


Best Regards,

Robert Krause

ICS Sociology, PhD Student
University of Groningen
Grote Rozenstraat 31,
Room B119
9712 TG Groningen, The Netherlands

messages.body_plain:
Hi Natalie,

I don't know about the mutual term in PNet, but the mutual term in the 
ergm package is kind of a misnomer. Intuitively, I would understand 
mutuality to be

h(N) = N_{ij} * N_{ji} * [X_{ij} == X_{ji}] + (1 - N_{ij}) * (1 - 
N_{ji}) * [X_{ij} == X_{ji}]

(i.e., reciprocation of ties and non-ties), while reciprocity should be 
merely the first part, i.e.,

h(N) = N_{ij} * N_{ji} * [X_{ij} == X_{ji}].

However, the ergm-terms help page indicates that the mutual term is 
actually based on this second definition. Just guessing, but perhaps 
that's the difference between the two implementations?

You could try to include the corresponding change statistic as a dyadic 
covariate (using an edgecov term) and check if that gets you closer to 
PNet. I think the change statistic would be

\delta^{<ij>} = N_{ji} * [X_{ij} == X_{ji}] - (1 - N_{ji}) * [X_{ij} == 
X_{ji}],

but you may want to double-check. That is, you could include an edgecov 
term with a covariate matrix that has values of 1 if the reciprocal tie 
exists and the attribute matches and -1 if it doesn't exist and there is 
a match (instead of including the mutual term). Just a thought, but 
maybe I'm wrong.

Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] directed networks in Add Health
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Quick question, short version: Has anyone had success modeling the full (directed) friend networks from Jefferson and Sunshine in Add Health (wave 1)?

Longer version: I'm aware that a number of publications have applied ERGMs to wave 1 Add Health data- but most (if not all) of these efforts have looked only at mutual friendships. I have a *vague* memory of asking someone about this ages ago, and it seemed, in addition to the theoretical motivation of looking at "stronger" (i.e. mutually validated) friendships, there was also a methodological backstory that folks were having a terrible time getting models for the full (directed) friend networks to converge. I am recently (and for the first time) diving into the data for these two schools myself- have spent some number of hours (unsuccessfully) pounding away at directed models- and am just wondering if this is a lost cause and I should use some undirected version (mutual or symmetrized) of the network instead. Or, if anyone has had success with it- advice would be appreciated! It's of course very possible I've missed a relevant publication or conversation.

Hope everyone is enjoying a great start to the summer.

Best wishes,
Kevin

P.S. Before sending, I did a quick search in the archives to make sure I'm not asking a dumb (i.e. already answered!) question. It looks like there was a similar exchange back in 2014 where, ironically, Martina and I were trying to help Karen figure out what was going wrong with her models for the exact same two schools. Karen/Martina, did you ever find a solution??! Could this have been just a directed/undirected issue, where for some reason the directed versions are especially slippery?

Kevin Lewis
Assistant Professor of Sociology
University of California, San Diego

Hi, Kevin.  This paper was focused on imputation (though you'll need it, 
if you are dealing with AH), but does employ the directed data:

Wang, Cheng; Butts, Carter T.; Hipp, John R.; and Jose, Rupa; and Lakon, 
Cynthia M. (2016). ``Multiple Imputation for Missing Edge Data: A 
Predictive Evaluation Method with Application to Add Health.'' Social 
Networks, 45, 89-98.

Cheng Wang has spent a lot of time on data wrangling with the full 
version of AH, so you might want to follow up with him if you have 
detailed data-related questions on the above.  Martina, Steve, Mark, and 
others have obviously been thinking very deeply about this data set for 
many years, so I'm sure they will have further suggestions.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] directed networks in Add Health
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin -

I don't know what work has been done on the directed AH networks (I 
haven't been following this literature lately), but I can say that the 
main methodological reason we did undirected was simply that back then 
we didn't have gwesp terms for directed networks available.  We do now.  
That said, the straight up gwesp term that appears in ergm, when used on 
directed networks, captures only one of the four types of directed gwesp 
terms, and I suspect you will need to have some larger combination of 
the four in there (and perhaps all four) to get model stability.

Since I rarely ever work with directed networks in my current research, 
I'm not sure of the syntax for the four terms, but Martina's grad 
student Li Wang is familiar with their current state, and I'm copying 
him here.

Cheers,
Steve

> Lakon, Cynthia M. (2016). ``Multiple Imputation for Missing Edge Data: 
> A Predictive Evaluation Method with Application to Add Health.'' 
> Social Networks, 45, 89-98.
>
> Cheng Wang has spent a lot of time on data wrangling with the full 
> version of AH, so you might want to follow up with him if you have 
> detailed data-related questions on the above.  Martina, Steve, Mark,
